text: A StatefulSet running PostgreSQL replicas uses `volumeClaimTemplates` with a StorageClass that has `reclaimPolicy: Delete`. A developer scales the StatefulSet from 5 to 3 replicas. What happens to the PersistentVolumeClaims (PVCs) associated with the deleted pods?
options: A. The PVCs for replicas 3 and 4 are automatically deleted along with their PersistentVolumes
B. The PVCs are orphaned and the StorageClass reclaim policy immediately triggers PV deletion
C. The PVCs are marked with a `deletionTimestamp` but remain until the StatefulSet is fully deleted
D. The PVCs remain intact and must be manually deleted; the underlying PVs are only reclaimed after PVC deletion

text: You configure a Pod Security Admission controller in `enforce` mode with the `restricted` profile at the namespace level. A Deployment specifies `securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true` and `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` but omits the `seccompProfile` field. What is the result when the Deployment is applied?
options: A. The Deployment is created but pods remain in `Pending` state until a seccomp profile is added
B. The entire Deployment is rejected at admission time because the `restricted` profile requires `seccompProfile` to be set to `RuntimeDefault` or `Localhost`
C. The Deployment object is created successfully, but the ReplicaSet fails to create pods due to the missing seccomp profile
D. The pods are created with a default seccomp profile automatically injected by the admission controller

text: An organization migrates a monolithic application to microservices. Service A calls Service B synchronously via HTTP REST. Under load, Service B becomes slow, causing Service A to exhaust its connection pool and cascade failures to Service C which depends on A. Which combination of patterns best prevents this cascading failure?
options: A. Rate limiting on Service B and retry logic with exponential backoff in Service A
B. Circuit breaker in Service A for calls to B, combined with bulkhead isolation to protect calls to C
C. Asynchronous messaging between all services with a dead-letter queue for failed messages
D. Increasing the connection pool size in Service A and adding horizontal pod autoscaling to Service B

text: A cluster has three nodes labeled `zone=us-east-1a`, `zone=us-east-1b`, and `zone=us-east-1c`. A Deployment with 3 replicas specifies `topologySpreadConstraints` with `maxSkew: 1`, `topologyKey: zone`, and `whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule`. Node `us-east-1c` becomes `NotReady`. When the Deployment is scaled to 6 replicas, how are the new pods distributed?
options: A. 3 pods on us-east-1a and 3 pods on us-east-1b; the constraint is satisfied across available zones
B. 2 pods on us-east-1a, 2 on us-east-1b, and the remaining 2 are Pending because scheduling on us-east-1c would violate the skew
C. 3 pods on us-east-1a, 3 on us-east-1b; the NotReady node is excluded from skew calculation
D. 4 pods schedule (2 per available zone) and 2 remain Pending because `maxSkew: 1` limits the difference between any two topology domains including the unavailable one

text: A microservices application uses OpenTelemetry for distributed tracing with a Jaeger backend. Service A (Go) calls Service B (Python) via gRPC. Traces show that spans from Service B are appearing as separate root traces instead of being children of Service A's spans. What is the most likely cause?
options: A. The Jaeger collector is dropping spans due to sampling rate limits configured at the agent level
B. Service A and B are using different OpenTelemetry SDK versions, causing incompatible span ID formats
C. The gRPC protocol does not support W3C Trace Context propagation and requires a custom carrier
D. Service B's OpenTelemetry SDK is not extracting the trace context propagation headers from the incoming gRPC metadata

text: A Service of type `ClusterIP` with `sessionAffinity: ClientIP` is configured with `sessionAffinityConfig.clientIP.timeoutSeconds: 10800`. The backend Deployment has 4 replicas behind this Service. A client pod makes requests every 2 seconds. After a rolling update replaces all backend pods, what happens to the client's session affinity?
options: A. The session affinity is preserved because `kube-proxy` maintains the affinity mapping to the new pod that replaced the old endpoint
B. Requests fail with connection refused until the `timeoutSeconds` expires and the affinity table is refreshed
C. The affinity is broken when the old pod's endpoint is removed; the next request is load-balanced to a new pod and a new affinity binding is created
D. The session affinity entry is migrated to the replacement pod automatically by the EndpointSlice controller

text: A Pod uses an `emptyDir` volume with `medium: Memory` and `sizeLimit: 256Mi`. The container writes 300Mi of data to this volume. What is the expected behavior?
options: A. The write succeeds but the pod is evicted by the kubelet when it detects the volume exceeds its size limit during periodic checks
B. The write operation fails with an I/O error when the 256Mi boundary is reached, similar to a full filesystem
C. The pod continues running since `sizeLimit` on memory-backed `emptyDir` is only advisory and not enforced
D. The container is OOM-killed because memory-backed `emptyDir` counts against the container's memory cgroup limit

text: A team uses Argo CD to manage deployments. They configure an `Application` resource with `syncPolicy.automated.prune: true` and `syncPolicy.automated.selfHeal: true`. A developer manually runs `kubectl scale deployment/api --replicas=10` in the target namespace. What happens next?
options: A. Argo CD detects the drift and scales the deployment back to the replica count defined in the Git repository within the next sync interval
B. Argo CD marks the application as `OutOfSync` but does not revert the change because scaling is excluded from self-heal by default
C. The manual change persists because Argo CD only watches for changes in Git, not for drift in the live cluster state
D. Argo CD creates a new Git commit reverting the replica count to maintain the single source of truth

text: A namespace has a `LimitRange` that sets `default.cpu: 500m` and `defaultRequest.cpu: 250m`. A ResourceQuota in the same namespace sets `limits.cpu: 4` and `requests.cpu: 2`. There are already 6 pods each using `requests.cpu: 250m` and `limits.cpu: 500m`. A new Deployment with 3 replicas is created without any resource specifications in the pod template. What happens?
options: A. All 3 replicas are created because the LimitRange defaults are injected and the total remains within quota
B. All 3 replicas are created because LimitRange-injected defaults are exempt from ResourceQuota enforcement
C. The Deployment is rejected entirely because creating any replica would require checking quota availability for all 3 simultaneously
D. Only 2 of the 3 replicas are created; the third is blocked because total CPU requests would exceed the ResourceQuota of 2 cores

text: A Kubernetes cluster uses Calico with `IPIP` encapsulation mode. A pod on Node A communicates with a pod on Node B in a different subnet. The network team reports that their firewall is blocking traffic between the nodes. Which protocol and port must be allowed for cross-subnet pod-to-pod communication?
options: A. UDP port 8472 for VXLAN encapsulation between Calico nodes
B. TCP port 9099 for Calico health checks and UDP port 51820 for WireGuard tunnels
C. IP protocol 4 (IP-in-IP) between the node IP addresses, plus TCP port 179 for BGP
D. IP protocol 47 (GRE) between node IP addresses and TCP port 179 for BGP route exchange

text: A multi-container pod has an init container that clones a Git repository into a shared `emptyDir` volume. The main application container mounts the same volume at `/app/config`. The pod is stuck in `Init:CrashLoopBackOff`. Logs show the init container completes successfully but exits with code 128. What is the most likely issue?
options: A. Exit code 128 indicates a Git fatal error — the repository URL is unreachable or authentication has failed
B. The `emptyDir` volume is not writable by the init container due to a `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` security context on the pod level
C. Exit code 128 indicates the init container received a SIGKILL, likely because it exceeded its memory resource limit during the git clone operation
D. The shared volume mount paths conflict because both containers specify the same `mountPath`, causing the init container to fail on restart

text: A Prometheus instance scraping 500 pods experiences high memory usage and slow queries. The team discovers that each pod exposes 2,000 unique time series with a label `request_id` that has unbounded cardinality. What is the correct approach to resolve this while maintaining useful metrics?
options: A. Increase Prometheus memory allocation and enable WAL compression to reduce the storage footprint of high-cardinality series
B. Switch to a push-based metrics model where pods send metrics directly to a time-series database that handles high cardinality natively
C. Configure `metric_relabel_configs` in the Prometheus scrape config to drop the `request_id` label before ingestion, and use distributed tracing for per-request data
D. Add `sample_limit` to the scrape config to cap the number of time series per target and configure recording rules to aggregate high-cardinality metrics

text: A Kubernetes node uses containerd as its container runtime with a default `RuntimeClass`. The security team requires that certain sensitive workloads run in gVisor sandboxes. A pod is created with `runtimeClassName: gvisor`, but it fails with `RuntimeClass "gvisor" not found`. What must be configured?
options: D. Add gVisor as a plugin in the kubelet configuration file and restart the kubelet; the `RuntimeClass` is auto-generated from the plugin registration
B. Create a `RuntimeClass` object with `handler: gvisor` and annotate the node with `runtime.kubernetes.io/gvisor=true` to enable the sandbox
C. Install the gVisor admission webhook, which automatically creates the `RuntimeClass` and configures containerd when it detects the `runtimeClassName` field
A. Install gVisor's `runsc` binary on the node, create a containerd runtime handler named `gvisor` in the containerd config, and create a `RuntimeClass` object in the cluster with `handler: runsc`

text: A cluster operator configures the `kube-apiserver` with `--audit-policy-file` pointing to an audit policy. The policy has a rule with `level: RequestResponse` for all resources in the `secrets` group. After deploying the policy, the audit log file grows rapidly and fills the disk. Which targeted change reduces log volume while still capturing security-relevant secret access?
options: A. Change the audit level to `Metadata` for secrets and add a specific `RequestResponse` rule only for `delete` and `create` verbs on secrets
B. Set `level: None` for secrets accessed by system service accounts and keep `RequestResponse` only for user-initiated requests
C. Reduce the `--audit-log-maxsize` and `--audit-log-maxbackup` flags to limit disk usage while keeping the same audit level
D. Change to `level: Request` globally and rely on external SIEM tools to reconstruct response bodies from request patterns

text: A platform team evaluates CNCF projects for their service mesh needs. They need mTLS between services, traffic splitting for canary deployments, and multi-cluster service discovery. They currently run Envoy sidecars manually. Which CNCF graduated project best fits as a control plane for their existing Envoy proxies?
options: A. Linkerd, because it is a graduated CNCF service mesh that provides mTLS, traffic splitting, and multi-cluster support with its own ultralight proxy
B. Open Service Mesh, because it is a CNCF project specifically designed as a lightweight Envoy-based control plane with SMI compatibility
C. Cilium, because it is a graduated CNCF project that provides eBPF-based service mesh with mTLS and multi-cluster networking
D. Istio, because it is a graduated CNCF project that uses Envoy as its data plane proxy and provides all three required features

text: A cluster uses CoreDNS for service discovery. A pod in namespace `team-a` tries to resolve `api-service.team-b.svc.cluster.local` but receives `NXDOMAIN`. The service exists and has endpoints. Running `nslookup api-service.team-b` from the same pod succeeds. What is the most likely cause of the FQDN resolution failure?
options: A. The pod's `/etc/resolv.conf` has `ndots:5` causing the short name to be resolved via search domains, but the FQDN bypasses search domain expansion and the trailing dot is missing
B. CoreDNS has a network policy blocking DNS queries that include the full `svc.cluster.local` suffix from the `team-a` namespace
C. The CoreDNS `Corefile` has a custom zone override for `cluster.local` that does not include the `team-b` namespace in its allowed zones
D. The FQDN query is being forwarded to the upstream DNS resolver instead of being handled by CoreDNS because it matches the forward plugin's catch-all rule

text: A Helm chart uses a `pre-install` hook to create a database schema migration Job. The hook has `helm.sh/hook-delete-policy: before-hook-creation`. After a failed `helm install`, the team runs `helm install` again with the same release name. The migration Job from the first attempt still exists in a `Failed` state. What happens?
options: A. Helm deletes the failed Job before creating a new one because `before-hook-creation` removes the previous hook resource on subsequent installs
B. Helm fails because the release name already exists in a `failed` state and must be uninstalled with `helm uninstall` first
C. The existing failed Job blocks the new hook Job creation, causing a naming conflict and a `helm install` error
D. Helm ignores the existing Job and creates a new Job with a random suffix appended to the name

text: An application pod requires access to the Kubernetes API to list pods in its own namespace. The pod uses a ServiceAccount with a bound Role and RoleBinding. The security team mandates that the automatically mounted service account token must have a 1-hour expiration and be bound to the pod's identity. Which approach satisfies these requirements?
options: A. Set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the pod and use a projected volume with a `serviceAccountToken` source specifying `expirationSeconds: 3600` and the API server audience
B. Create a TokenRequest API call from an init container to generate a short-lived token, store it in a shared `emptyDir` volume, and configure the application to read from that path
C. Configure the ServiceAccount with the annotation `kubernetes.io/enforce-mountable-secrets` and set the token's `exp` claim via a custom admission webhook
D. Enable the `BoundServiceAccountTokenVolume` feature gate (disabled by default) and set the `--service-account-max-token-expiration` flag on the API server to 1 hour

text: A team deploys a Knative Serving application that handles webhook events. The application experiences cold start latency of 8 seconds when scaling from zero. The SLA requires responses within 3 seconds. The team wants to minimize resource usage while meeting the SLA. What is the optimal Knative configuration?
options: A. Set `minScale: 1` in the Knative Service revision template to keep at least one instance warm at all times
B. Configure `scale-to-zero-grace-period` to 30 minutes globally in the Knative config-autoscaler ConfigMap
C. Set the `initialScale` annotation to 3 and enable `allow-zero-initial-scale` to handle burst traffic after the first cold start
D. Use `minScale: 0` with `target-burst-capacity: -1` to disable the activator buffering and let the autoscaler handle scaling decisions directly

text: A Deployment with `strategy.type: RollingUpdate`, `maxSurge: 1`, and `maxUnavailable: 0` has 5 replicas. A new image version is rolled out, but the new pods fail readiness probes. What is the state of the rollout?
options: A. The rollout creates 1 new pod (surge), which never becomes Ready; the 5 old pods remain running and serving traffic; the rollout is stalled indefinitely
B. The rollout continues creating new pods one at a time regardless of readiness because `maxUnavailable: 0` only prevents old pod deletion
C. The rollout immediately rolls back to the previous version after the `progressDeadlineSeconds` is exceeded
D. The rollout creates 6 pods (5 old + 1 new), then begins terminating old pods because the total pod count exceeds the desired replica count

text: A pod with two containers — `app` (port 8080) and `sidecar` (port 9090) — is in `Running` state, but the `app` container constantly restarts. Logs show `app` exits with `Error: listen EADDRINUSE :::8080`. The `sidecar` container is configured to listen on port 9090. What is the most likely cause?
options: A. The `sidecar` container has a secondary listener binding to port 8080 in addition to its primary port 9090
B. A previous instance of the `app` container has not fully released port 8080 due to TCP TIME_WAIT, and the restart happens faster than the socket timeout
C. The pod has a `hostNetwork: true` setting, and another pod on the same node is already bound to port 8080
D. Both containers share the same network namespace, and the `app` container's `livenessProbe` on port 8080 creates a listener conflict during probe execution

text: A microservices platform uses the Saga pattern for distributed transactions. An order service starts a saga that involves payment, inventory, and shipping services. The payment succeeds, the inventory reservation succeeds, but the shipping service fails. How should the saga orchestrator handle this failure?
options: A. Retry the shipping service call with exponential backoff until it succeeds, keeping the saga open indefinitely
B. Execute compensating transactions in reverse order: release the inventory reservation, then refund the payment
C. Mark the saga as partially complete and let an eventual consistency mechanism reconcile the state across services later
D. Roll back using a two-phase commit protocol across all three services to ensure atomic reversal

text: A cluster administrator creates a custom `PriorityClass` with `globalDefault: true` and `value: 100`. The cluster already has the system-provided `system-cluster-critical` (value 2000000000) and `system-node-critical` (value 2000001000) priority classes. A pod is created without specifying a `priorityClassName`. What priority value is assigned?
options: A. Priority value 0, because only one `globalDefault` PriorityClass can exist and the system ignores user-created defaults
B. Priority value 2000000000, because system priority classes take precedence over user-defined global defaults
C. Priority value 100, because the custom PriorityClass with `globalDefault: true` applies to all pods without explicit priority class assignment
D. No priority is assigned and the pod creation fails with a validation error about ambiguous default priority

text: A StatefulSet uses a PVC with `accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]` backed by an AWS EBS volume. The pod is rescheduled to a node in a different availability zone. The pod is stuck in `Pending`. What is the root cause and correct resolution?
options: D. The StorageClass must have `allowedTopologies` set to all availability zones for the volume to be mountable across zones
B. EBS volumes require `ReadWriteMany` access mode for cross-zone mounting; change the access mode in the PVC spec
C. The PV is still attached to the old node; manually detach it using `kubectl patch pv` with the `volumeattachments` finalizer removed
A. EBS volumes are zone-scoped; add a `nodeAffinity` to the StatefulSet matching the volume's AZ, or use a StorageClass with `volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer`

text:
A NetworkPolicy with the following spec is applied to namespace `production`:

```yaml
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          env: production
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          role: frontend
    ports:
    - port: 443
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: database
```

A pod labeled `role: frontend` in a namespace labeled `env: staging` sends a request to the `api` pod on port 443. Is the traffic allowed?
options: A. Yes, because the `podSelector` matches the source pod's label `role: frontend` regardless of namespace
B. No, because the `namespaceSelector` and `podSelector` under the same `from` entry form an AND condition — both must match
C. Yes, because `namespaceSelector` and `podSelector` in the same array element are evaluated as an OR condition
D. No, because the egress policy does not include a rule allowing responses back to the frontend pod

text: A cluster uses a DaemonSet-based Fluentd deployment for log collection. Application pods write structured JSON logs to stdout. The Fluentd configuration parses logs using a regex parser. After a Kubernetes upgrade, logs from some pods appear as raw unparsed strings. Investigation reveals these pods use the containerd runtime. What is the issue?
options: A. Containerd uses the CRI log format (`<timestamp> <stream> <flags> <log>`) which wraps the JSON output, causing the regex parser to fail on the CRI envelope
B. Containerd writes logs in binary protobuf format instead of text, requiring a specialized Fluentd input plugin
C. The Kubernetes upgrade changed the log directory from `/var/log/containers/` to `/var/log/pods/`, and Fluentd is reading from the old path
D. Containerd rotates log files more aggressively, and Fluentd loses its position tracking when files are rotated

text: The `kube-controller-manager` runs multiple controllers in a single process. The `--controllers` flag is set to `*,-bootstrapsigner,-tokencleaner`. A new CRD is installed with a corresponding custom controller deployed as a Deployment. Which statement is correct about the interaction between built-in and custom controllers?
options: A. The custom controller must register itself with the `kube-controller-manager` via the controller registration API to avoid conflicts
B. The `--controllers` flag must include the custom controller's name prefixed with a `+` to enable it alongside the disabled controllers
C. Built-in controllers have priority over custom controllers for the same resource, potentially causing reconciliation conflicts on CRDs

D. The custom controller operates independently using its own informer cache and watch connections; the `--controllers` flag only affects built-in controllers within the `kube-controller-manager` process

text: A team performs a canary deployment using Istio VirtualService traffic splitting. The canary receives 10% of traffic. After monitoring for 30 minutes, error rates on the canary are 5x higher than the stable version. The Istio `VirtualService` weight is updated to send 0% to the canary. However, some users still report errors from the canary for several minutes after the change. Why?
options: A. Envoy sidecar proxies cache the VirtualService routing configuration and require a proxy restart to pick up the new weights
B. The Istio control plane (istiod) takes time to push the updated configuration to all Envoy sidecars in the mesh
C. Long-lived HTTP/2 or gRPC connections established before the weight change continue to route to the canary until those connections are closed
D. The `VirtualService` weight change requires the canary Deployment to be scaled to 0 replicas to actually stop receiving traffic

text: An OPA Gatekeeper `ConstraintTemplate` enforces that all containers must have resource limits set. A pod with an init container specifying resource limits and a main container without limits is submitted. What is the result?
options: A. The pod is admitted because Gatekeeper only validates the primary container spec, not init containers
B. The pod is rejected because Gatekeeper evaluates all containers in the pod spec, including init containers, ephemeral containers, and regular containers
C. The result depends on the Rego policy in the ConstraintTemplate — if it iterates over `input.review.object.spec.containers` only, init containers are not checked
D. The pod is admitted but flagged with a warning annotation because Gatekeeper uses `warn` enforcement for partial compliance

text: A team migrating to cloud native architecture needs to decide on a service communication strategy. Service A (order processing) must call Service B (payment gateway) with guaranteed delivery even if B is temporarily unavailable. Service A also calls Service C (notification) where occasional message loss is acceptable. Which architecture best fits these requirements?
options: A. Synchronous REST calls for both B and C with retry middleware and circuit breakers to handle failures
D. Service mesh sidecar proxies handling automatic retries for both B and C, with configurable retry budgets per destination
C. gRPC streaming for A-to-B with server-side retry interceptors, and webhooks for A-to-C notifications
B. Asynchronous messaging with a persistent message queue for A-to-B communication, and fire-and-forget async events for A-to-C

text: An operator creates a `ValidatingWebhookConfiguration` with `failurePolicy: Fail` and a `namespaceSelector` that matches all namespaces. The webhook service goes down. What impact does this have on the cluster?
options: A. Only create and update operations on the matched resources are blocked; read operations and deletions continue normally
B. The API server automatically switches to `Ignore` failure policy after a configurable timeout to prevent cluster lockout
C. All API operations matching the webhook's rules are rejected with a 500 error, including operations in `kube-system`, potentially making the cluster unmanageable
D. Operations are queued by the API server for up to 30 seconds and then processed without webhook validation if the service does not recover

text: A container image built with a multi-stage Dockerfile uses `FROM scratch` as the final stage. The image runs a statically compiled Go binary. When deployed to Kubernetes, `kubectl exec` into the container fails with `OCI runtime exec failed: exec failed: unable to start container process: exec: "/bin/sh": stat /bin/sh: no such file or directory`. How should the team enable debugging for this pod?
options: A. Add a `distroless/debug` base image as the final stage instead of `scratch` to include a busybox shell
B. Use `kubectl debug` to create an ephemeral debug container with a shell image that shares the pod's process namespace
C. Mount a ConfigMap containing a shell binary at `/bin/sh` in the container's volume mounts
D. Rebuild the image with `FROM alpine` and include `RUN apk add --no-cache bash` in the final stage

text: A Prometheus alerting rule fires when `rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]) / rate(http_requests_total[5m]) > 0.05` for 10 minutes. The SRE team notices the alert fires during a deployment window when traffic drops to near-zero, even though only 1 request out of 20 returned a 500 error. What adjustment prevents false positives during low-traffic periods?
options: A. Change the alert threshold from 5% to 10% to account for statistical insignificance during low-traffic windows
B. Replace `rate()` with `increase()` to use absolute counts instead of per-second rates, which are less sensitive to low volume
C. Increase the `for` duration from 10 minutes to 30 minutes so the alert waits for traffic to normalize before firing
D. Add a minimum request rate condition: `rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]) / rate(http_requests_total[5m]) > 0.05 AND rate(http_requests_total[5m]) > 1`

text: A pod has a `readinessProbe` with `httpGet` on path `/healthz`, port 8080, `periodSeconds: 5`, `failureThreshold: 3`, and `successThreshold: 2`. The application starts returning 503 from `/healthz`. How long after the first failed probe does the pod stop receiving Service traffic?
options: A. 5 seconds — the first failure immediately marks the pod as not ready
B. 15 seconds — three consecutive failures at 5-second intervals trigger the not-ready state
C. 10 seconds — the `failureThreshold` of 3 means 3 failures, but the first probe was at time 0 so it takes 2 intervals
D. 10 seconds — the second failure at time 10s triggers removal because the threshold counts from the initial success state

text: A cluster uses kube-proxy in IPVS mode. A Service with `sessionAffinity: None` has 3 backend pods. The IPVS scheduler is set to `rr` (round-robin). One pod consistently handles 70% of the traffic instead of the expected 33%. Network captures show the traffic comes from a small number of source IPs behind a corporate NAT gateway. What explains this distribution?
options: A. IPVS round-robin is per-connection, not per-packet; the NAT gateway's connection pooling reuses a small number of connections, skewing distribution
B. IPVS in `rr` mode has a warmup period where it favors the first registered backend until all backends have received at least one connection
C. The overloaded pod has the lowest IP address and IPVS round-robin starts from the lowest IP for each new connection cycle
D. kube-proxy's IPVS implementation uses consistent hashing internally even when `rr` is configured, causing sticky routing for the same source IPs

text: A pod has `resources.requests.cpu: 4` and `resources.limits.cpu: 4` with `resources.requests.memory: 8Gi` and `resources.limits.memory: 8Gi`. What QoS class is assigned, and what is the eviction priority during node memory pressure?
options: A. `Guaranteed` QoS — this pod is the last to be evicted during memory pressure because requests equal limits for all resources
B. `Burstable` QoS — because the CPU value of 4 exceeds the typical node allocatable, the pod is classified as burstable
C. `Guaranteed` QoS — but it can still be evicted before `BestEffort` pods if its actual memory consumption exceeds the pod's `limits.memory`
D. `Guaranteed` QoS — it is evicted after `Burstable` pods but before `BestEffort` pods during memory pressure

text: A CI/CD pipeline uses Tekton Pipelines to build and deploy an application. A `Pipeline` has three sequential `Tasks`: `git-clone`, `build-image`, and `deploy`. The `build-image` task needs the source code from `git-clone` and must pass the built image tag to `deploy`. Which Tekton mechanism correctly passes data between these tasks?
options: A. Use `PipelineResources` of type `git` and `image` to automatically wire inputs and outputs between tasks
B. Mount a shared `PersistentVolumeClaim` in all tasks and write/read data to agreed-upon file paths; use environment variables for the image tag
D. Use Tekton `Conditions` to evaluate the output of each task and dynamically inject parameters into the next task
C. Use `Workspaces` for sharing the cloned source code and `Task Results` to pass the image tag string from `build-image` to `deploy`

text: A Kubernetes cluster runs version 1.29. A CRD is created with two stored versions: `v1alpha1` and `v1beta1`, with `v1beta1` as the served and storage version. A conversion webhook is configured. An existing `v1alpha1` resource is stored in etcd. A client requests the resource via the `v1beta1` API. What happens?
options: A. The API server reads the `v1alpha1` object from etcd and returns it directly since both versions are stored; the client must handle version differences
B. The API server serves a cached `v1beta1` version that was pre-converted when the CRD version was updated
C. The API server rejects the request because resources stored in `v1alpha1` format cannot be served via the `v1beta1` endpoint without first running a storage migration
D. The API server reads the `v1alpha1` object from etcd, calls the conversion webhook to convert it to `v1beta1`, and returns the converted object to the client

text: A headless Service (`clusterIP: None`) is created for a StatefulSet with 3 replicas named `web-0`, `web-1`, and `web-2` in namespace `default`. The Service name is `web-svc`. A pod in the same namespace performs a DNS lookup for `web-svc.default.svc.cluster.local`. What DNS records are returned?
options: A. A single A record pointing to the kube-proxy virtual IP that load-balances across all three pod IPs
B. A CNAME record pointing to the StatefulSet's stable network identity, which then resolves to the current leader pod
C. Three A records, one for each pod IP, allowing the client's DNS resolver to perform client-side load balancing
D. Three SRV records mapping to `web-0.web-svc.default.svc.cluster.local`, `web-1.web-svc.default.svc.cluster.local`, and `web-2.web-svc.default.svc.cluster.local`

text:
A pod in state `CrashLoopBackOff` has the following events:
```
Warning  BackOff  kubelet  Back-off restarting failed container
Normal   Pulled   kubelet  Container image already present on machine
Warning  Failed   kubelet  Error: failed to create containerd task: failed to create shim task: OCI runtime create failed: runc create failed: unable to start container process: exec: "app": executable file not found in $PATH
```
The Dockerfile's last line is `CMD ["app"]`. The image was built successfully. What is the root cause?
options: A. The binary `app` was compiled for a different CPU architecture (e.g., ARM) than the node's architecture (e.g., AMD64)
B. The `CMD` instruction should use shell form (`CMD app`) instead of exec form (`CMD ["app"]`) to resolve the binary via `$PATH`
C. The binary `app` is present in the build stage but was not copied to the final stage in a multi-stage Dockerfile, so it does not exist in the runtime image
D. The container's `securityContext` has `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`, preventing the runtime from accessing the binary at its path

text: A team designs their Kubernetes deployment strategy around the principle of immutable infrastructure. Which practice violates this principle?
options: A. Using `kubectl exec` to SSH into a running container and apply a hotfix patch directly to the application binary
B. Building a new container image for every code change and deploying it through a rolling update
C. Storing application configuration in ConfigMaps mounted as volumes that trigger pod restarts on change
D. Using init containers to download and cache static assets from a CDN into an `emptyDir` volume at pod startup

text: A Deployment runs pods with a `preStop` lifecycle hook that sends a SIGTERM to the application and waits for graceful shutdown. The pod also has `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30`. The `preStop` hook takes 25 seconds to complete. After the hook finishes, how much time does the application have to respond to the subsequent SIGTERM from the kubelet?
options: A. 30 seconds — the `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` resets after the `preStop` hook completes
B. 5 seconds — the `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` includes the time spent in the `preStop` hook, leaving only the remaining time for SIGTERM handling
C. 25 seconds — the kubelet deducts the `preStop` hook duration and adds a 20-second buffer for SIGTERM handling
D. Indefinitely — once the `preStop` hook signals graceful shutdown, the kubelet waits for the process to exit naturally

text: A pod's container runs as UID 1000 and has `securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`. The application needs to write temporary files to `/tmp` and log files to `/var/log/app`. Which volume configuration allows the application to function while maintaining the read-only filesystem security posture?
options: A. Mount two `emptyDir` volumes at `/tmp` and `/var/log/app`; the read-only root filesystem policy does not apply to mounted volumes
B. Add `allowedHostPaths` entries for `/tmp` and `/var/log/app` in the PodSecurityPolicy to whitelist writable paths
C. Set `readOnlyRootFilesystem: false` but use an OPA policy to restrict writes to only `/tmp` and `/var/log/app` paths
D. Use `subPath` mounts from a single `emptyDir` volume to both paths, which bypasses the read-only constraint

text: A microservices system uses the API Gateway pattern. The gateway handles authentication, rate limiting, and request routing. During peak traffic, the gateway becomes a bottleneck with p99 latency exceeding 2 seconds. Adding more gateway replicas improves throughput but not latency. What is the most likely architectural issue?
options: A. The gateway is performing synchronous JWT validation against an external identity provider for every request, adding network round-trip latency
B. The gateway replicas share a single database connection pool for rate-limiting state, creating lock contention
C. Adding replicas increases the total number of connections to backend services, causing backend connection exhaustion
D. The gateway's load balancer uses layer-4 (TCP) routing, causing uneven connection distribution among gateway replicas

text: A pod specifies `affinity.podAntiAffinity.requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` with `topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname` and a `labelSelector` matching itself. The Deployment has 4 replicas and the cluster has 3 nodes. What happens?
options: A. All 4 replicas are scheduled — the anti-affinity is evaluated per-replica and does not prevent co-location since they are part of the same Deployment
B. 3 replicas are scheduled (one per node) and the 4th remains Pending because no node can satisfy the anti-affinity constraint
C. The scheduler ignores the anti-affinity for the 4th replica and co-locates it with an existing replica on the least-loaded node
D. All 4 replicas remain Pending because the anti-affinity creates a circular dependency that the scheduler cannot resolve

text: A platform team implements distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry. They configure a `sampling.ratio` of 0.01 (1%) in production. A critical user reports a failed transaction, but the trace for that transaction was not sampled. What tracing strategy would capture this trace while maintaining the low sampling overhead?
options: A. Switch to 100% sampling and use tail-based sampling at the collector to only retain traces with errors or high latency
B. Increase the head-based sampling ratio to 10% and accept the additional overhead for better coverage of error scenarios
C. Configure the OpenTelemetry SDK with a composite sampler: always sample traces with error status codes and probabilistically sample the rest at 1%
D. Use a separate trace pipeline for error cases that sends traces directly to the backend, bypassing the sampling configuration

text:
A namespace has two ResourceQuotas:
- `quota-compute`: `requests.cpu: 4, limits.cpu: 8`
- `quota-objects`: `count/deployments.apps: 10, count/services: 5`

When a new Deployment is created, which quotas must have available capacity?
options: A. Only `quota-objects` must have capacity for the Deployment count; `quota-compute` is checked only when pods are created by the Deployment's ReplicaSet
B. Both quotas are checked simultaneously — `quota-objects` for the Deployment count and `quota-compute` for the pods that will be created
C. Only `quota-objects` is checked at Deployment creation time; `quota-compute` is checked separately when the ReplicaSet controller creates individual pods
D. Neither quota is checked at Deployment creation — all quota enforcement is deferred to pod scheduling time

text: A multi-tenant cluster uses Cilium as the CNI with `HostPort` support. Tenant A's pod uses `hostPort: 8080`. Tenant B deploys a pod also requesting `hostPort: 8080`. Both pods are scheduled on the same node. What happens?
options: A. Both pods start successfully because Cilium uses network namespaces to isolate `hostPort` bindings per tenant
B. Tenant B's pod fails to schedule on that node because the scheduler checks `hostPort` conflicts as part of port allocation during scheduling
C. Both pods are scheduled, but Tenant B's pod enters `CrashLoopBackOff` because the port is already bound at the host level
D. Cilium's network policy engine blocks Tenant B's `hostPort` request at the CNI level, returning an error to the kubelet

text: A highly available Kubernetes cluster has 3 control-plane nodes, each running `kube-apiserver`, `kube-controller-manager`, and `kube-scheduler`. How do the controller-manager and scheduler coordinate to prevent duplicate work across the 3 instances?
options: A. All three instances process work simultaneously using distributed locking on individual resources in etcd
B. Each instance watches a partitioned subset of namespaces, dividing the workload using consistent hashing
C. The API server round-robins controller requests across the three instances using an internal load balancer
D. They use leader election via Lease objects in the `kube-system` namespace; only the leader instance actively reconciles while others are on standby

text: A team containerizes a legacy application that stores user sessions in local filesystem files under `/var/sessions`. The application runs as a Deployment with 3 replicas behind a ClusterIP Service. Users report that they are randomly logged out. What is the root cause and the best cloud native solution?
options: A. Use a `ReadWriteMany` PersistentVolume shared across all replicas so all pods can access the same session files
B. Replace local filesystem session storage with an external Redis or Memcached cluster, and configure the Service with `sessionAffinity: ClientIP` as a transitional measure
C. Convert the Deployment to a StatefulSet so each replica has a dedicated PersistentVolume for its session files
D. Add `sessionAffinity: ClientIP` to the Service to ensure users always hit the same pod where their session is stored

text: A CSI driver provides block storage volumes. A pod requests a PVC with `volumeMode: Block` and mounts it using `volumeDevices` instead of `volumeMounts`. Inside the container, the device appears at `/dev/xvda`. The application attempts to mount the device with `mount /dev/xvda /data` and fails with `mount: /dev/xvda: can't find in /etc/fstab`. What is the correct approach?
options: A. Add an entry to `/etc/fstab` inside the container image for the block device path and filesystem type
B. Use an init container to run `mkfs.ext4 /dev/xvda` before the application container starts, then mount in the app container
C. Change the PVC to `volumeMode: Filesystem` which instructs the CSI driver to format and mount the volume automatically via kubelet
D. Add a `formatOptions` field to the StorageClass parameters to pre-format the block device before it is attached to the pod

text:
An Ingress resource specifies two rules:
1. `host: api.example.com`, path `/v1` -> Service `api-v1:80`
2. `host: api.example.com`, path `/v2` -> Service `api-v2:80`

The Ingress controller is nginx. A request to `https://api.example.com/v2/users` returns a 404 from the `api-v2` service. The same request directly to the `api-v2` Service ClusterIP works. What is the likely issue?
options: A. The Ingress controller forwards the request with the original path `/v2/users`, but the `api-v2` application expects requests at `/users` without the `/v2` prefix
B. The Ingress resource needs `pathType: Prefix` instead of the default `Exact` to match `/v2/users` under the `/v2` rule
C. The nginx Ingress controller strips TLS before forwarding, and the `api-v2` service rejects non-HTTPS connections
D. The Ingress controller cannot route to two different services under the same host and overlapping path prefixes

text: A FinOps team analyzes Kubernetes cluster costs and finds that development namespaces consume 60% of cluster resources but only utilize 15% of what they request. Production namespaces request 30% and utilize 28%. What combination of strategies best optimizes costs without impacting production?
options: A. Implement cluster autoscaler with aggressive scale-down settings and use Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) in `UpdateMode: Auto` for all namespaces
B. Apply `LimitRange` objects in development namespaces to enforce lower default requests, use VPA in `UpdateMode: Off` (recommendation-only) for dev workloads, and keep production unchanged
C. Set ResourceQuotas in development namespaces to cap total requests at 30% of current levels and enable `LimitRange` with `max` constraints
D. Move all development workloads to spot/preemptible nodes using taints and tolerations, and right-size requests based on VPA recommendations

text: A StatefulSet with `podManagementPolicy: OrderedReady` and 5 replicas is being updated with `updateStrategy.type: RollingUpdate` and `partition: 3`. What is the effect of the `partition` parameter?
options: A. Only pods with ordinal index >= 3 (pods 3 and 4) are updated with the new spec; pods 0, 1, and 2 retain the old spec
B. The update proceeds in batches of 3 pods at a time, starting from the highest ordinal
C. Pods 0, 1, and 2 are updated first, then pods 3 and 4 are updated after the first group is ready
D. The partition creates two independent groups that can be updated and rolled back separately

text: A node runs containerd with the default `overlayfs` snapshotter. A pod with 3 containers sharing the same base image (`ubuntu:22.04`) is scheduled to this node. How does containerd handle the image layers for these 3 containers?
options: A. Each container gets its own complete copy of all image layers, consuming 3x the storage of a single container
B. The base image layers are shared read-only across all 3 containers via overlayfs, with each container getting its own thin read-write upper layer
C. The first container pulls the image and subsequent containers use a copy-on-write clone of the first container's filesystem
D. Containerd deduplicates layers using content-addressable storage but extracts separate snapshots for each container for isolation

text: A controller watches Custom Resources and uses `metadata.resourceVersion` for optimistic concurrency. Two controller replicas read the same CR (resourceVersion: "1000"), each modify a different field, and attempt to update. What happens?
options: A. Both updates succeed because they modify different fields, and the API server merges the changes automatically
B. The first update succeeds (resourceVersion becomes "1001"); the second fails with a `409 Conflict` because its resourceVersion ("1000") is stale
C. The API server queues both updates and applies them sequentially, incrementing the resourceVersion for each
D. Both updates fail because only the resource owner (identified by `metadata.ownerReferences`) can update Custom Resources

text: A pod runs normally for hours, then is suddenly terminated with reason `OOMKilled`. The container's `resources.limits.memory` is set to `512Mi`. Prometheus metrics show the container's resident memory (RSS) peaked at 480Mi, well below the limit. What explains the OOM kill despite being under the memory limit?
options: A. The kernel's memory cgroup accounting includes page cache used by the container, which combined with RSS exceeded the 512Mi cgroup limit
B. The kubelet's eviction threshold triggered before the container reached its limit, killing the largest memory consumer
C. The container spawned child processes whose memory is not tracked by Prometheus but is counted in the cgroup total
D. Memory fragmentation caused the kernel to report higher memory usage than actual RSS, triggering the OOM kill

text: A team wants to implement a GitOps workflow with automated drift detection, multi-cluster support, and the ability to deploy both Kubernetes manifests and Helm charts. They need the tool to provide a web UI for visualizing application state. Which CNCF project best meets all requirements?
options: A. Flux CD — it provides GitOps reconciliation with multi-cluster support, Helm controller, and a built-in web dashboard
B. Jenkins X — it provides cloud native CI/CD with GitOps capabilities, Helm deployments, and a pipeline visualization UI
D. Keptn — it provides cloud native application lifecycle management with GitOps, multi-cluster support, and quality gate visualization
C. Argo CD — it is a CNCF graduated project providing GitOps with drift detection, multi-cluster management, Helm support, and a comprehensive web UI

text: A cluster uses the `descheduler` to rebalance pods. A Deployment has `podAntiAffinity` with `preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` (weight 100) and `topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname`. After a node is added to the cluster, 3 of the 4 Deployment replicas remain on 2 nodes while the new node is empty. What does the descheduler's `RemoveDuplicates` strategy do?
options: A. It evicts one pod from the node with 2 replicas, allowing the scheduler to place it on the new empty node respecting the anti-affinity preference
B. It evicts all pods and lets the scheduler redistribute them evenly across all three nodes
C. It does nothing because `RemoveDuplicates` only handles pods owned by the same ReplicaSet on the same node, not across nodes
D. It evicts pods only if the `preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` anti-affinity score would improve after rebalancing

text: A container image is signed using `cosign` and pushed to a registry. A Kyverno `ClusterPolicy` with `verifyImages` rule enforces signature verification. A deployment references the image by tag (`:latest`). The image is re-pushed with a different digest but the same tag. Does the existing running pod get affected, and does a new pod creation succeed?
options: A. The existing pod is unaffected (uses the original digest); new pod creation succeeds only if the re-pushed image is also signed with a valid cosign signature
B. The existing pod is terminated because the image digest it runs no longer matches the tag; new pod creation is blocked by Kyverno
C. Both the existing pod and new pods are unaffected because Kyverno only checks signatures during policy creation, not during pod admission
D. The existing pod continues running; new pod creation fails because Kyverno detects the tag-to-digest mapping changed and considers it a supply chain attack

text: A team implements blue-green deployment using two Deployments (`blue` and `green`) and a Service that selects pods by a `version` label. The current production traffic goes to `blue`. After deploying the new version to `green` and running smoke tests, the team switches the Service selector from `version: blue` to `version: green`. Users report brief 503 errors during the switch. What causes the errors?
options: A. The EndpointSlice controller takes time to propagate the new endpoints to kube-proxy on all nodes, creating a window where some nodes have stale routing rules
B. The Service selector change causes all existing TCP connections to be immediately terminated, and clients reconnecting experience 503s
C. kube-proxy's iptables/IPVS rules are updated asynchronously, and there is a brief period where the rules point to the old blue pods that no longer match the selector
D. The green pods' readiness probes have not yet been verified by the EndpointSlice controller at the moment of the selector switch

text: A pod has two containers: `main` and `sidecar`. The pod is terminating. The `main` container has a `preStop` hook that takes 10 seconds. The `sidecar` has no lifecycle hooks. The pod has `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30`. In what order do the termination steps occur?
options: A. The `main` container's `preStop` hook runs first, then both containers receive SIGTERM simultaneously after the hook completes
B. Both containers receive SIGTERM simultaneously; the `main` container's `preStop` hook runs in parallel with the SIGTERM delivery
C. The `main` container's `preStop` hook and the `sidecar`'s SIGTERM are initiated simultaneously; after the `preStop` completes, `main` also receives SIGTERM
D. The `sidecar` container is terminated first, then the `main` container's `preStop` hook runs, followed by SIGTERM to `main`

text: A cluster uses Kubernetes Service of type `NodePort` with `nodePort: 30080`. The cluster has 10 nodes but only 2 nodes run the backend pods. A client external to the cluster sends a request to Node 5 (which has no backend pod) at port 30080. What is the network path of the request?
options: A. Node 5 drops the request because there is no local backend pod and the default `externalTrafficPolicy` is `Local`
B. Node 5's kube-proxy forwards the request to one of the 2 nodes with backend pods via DNAT, adding SNAT to preserve the return path
C. Node 5 responds with a TCP RST because NodePort services only listen on nodes with backend pods
D. The request is forwarded to the Service's ClusterIP, which then distributes it to a backend pod without any NAT

text: The kubelet on a worker node loses connectivity to the API server. The node's lease in the `kube-node-lease` namespace expires. After `node-monitor-grace-period` (default 40s) passes, what sequence of actions does the control plane take?
options: A. The node controller marks the node as `NotReady` immediately; after `pod-eviction-timeout` the node controller begins evicting pods by creating deletion entries

B. The node controller marks the node as `Unknown` after the grace period; after additional taint-based eviction delay, pods are evicted unless they tolerate the `node.kubernetes.io/unreachable` taint
C. The node controller deletes the node object; the scheduler reschedules all pods to other nodes immediately
D. The node controller adds the `node.kubernetes.io/not-ready` taint; pods without a matching toleration are evicted after `tolerationSeconds` expires

text: A KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaler) `ScaledObject` is configured to scale a Deployment based on an Azure Service Bus queue length. The `ScaledObject` specifies `minReplicaCount: 0` and `maxReplicaCount: 20`. The queue currently has 500 messages and the trigger threshold is 10 messages per replica. How does KEDA determine the target replica count?
options: A. KEDA sets the target to 50 replicas (500/10), but the `maxReplicaCount` caps it at 20
B. KEDA sets the target to 20 replicas immediately because the queue backlog exceeds the maximum capacity
C. KEDA scales linearly: 1 replica, then 2, then 4, doubling every scaling interval until reaching 20 or the queue is drained
D. KEDA calculates 50 replicas but scales to 20 in a single step, then pauses scaling until the next evaluation interval

text: A team configures Prometheus `ServiceMonitor` resources for their application. The `ServiceMonitor` selects services with label `monitoring: enabled`. The Prometheus Operator's `Prometheus` CR has `serviceMonitorSelector: {}` (empty selector, matches all). However, metrics from the application are not being scraped. What is the most likely cause?
options: A. The `ServiceMonitor` and the `Prometheus` CR are in different namespaces, and `serviceMonitorNamespaceSelector` is not configured to include the `ServiceMonitor`'s namespace
B. The empty selector `{}` means "match nothing"; it should be omitted entirely to match all `ServiceMonitor` resources
C. The application's Service does not have the `monitoring: enabled` label, so the `ServiceMonitor` does not discover any endpoints
D. Prometheus needs to be restarted after a `ServiceMonitor` is created because it does not watch for new `ServiceMonitor` resources dynamically

text: A Deployment uses `strategy.type: Recreate`. The Deployment has a `PodDisruptionBudget` (PDB) with `minAvailable: 1`. During an update, the Deployment controller attempts to delete all existing pods before creating new ones. How does the PDB interact with the Recreate strategy?
options: A. The PDB prevents the Recreate strategy from deleting all pods; at least 1 pod remains running throughout the update
B. The PDB is ignored during Deployment-initiated updates because the Deployment controller is not subject to PDB enforcement; PDBs only apply to voluntary evictions via the Eviction API
C. The Deployment controller deletes pods one at a time, respecting the PDB, effectively converting the Recreate strategy to a RollingUpdate
D. The update is blocked entirely because the Recreate strategy conflicts with the PDB, and the Deployment reports a failure condition

text: A pod's `livenessProbe` uses `exec` to run a script `/healthcheck.sh` that queries a local database connection. The probe has `timeoutSeconds: 5` and `periodSeconds: 10`. The pod is being restarted frequently. Logs show the application is healthy, but `kubectl describe` shows `Liveness probe failed: command timed out`. Node monitoring shows high CPU load on the node. What is the issue?
options: A. The `/healthcheck.sh` script has a database query that occasionally takes longer than 5 seconds due to table locks
B. Under high CPU load, the node's kubelet cannot fork the exec process within the `timeoutSeconds` window, causing the probe to time out before the script even starts
C. The exec probe launches a new process that competes for CPU with the application container, and under high node CPU pressure, the probe process is throttled by the cgroup CPU limit
D. The kubelet's probe worker pool is exhausted due to the high number of pods on the node, delaying probe execution beyond the timeout

text: A microservices architecture uses the Strangler Fig pattern to migrate from a monolith. An API gateway routes traffic: `/api/orders/*` goes to the new Orders microservice, while all other paths go to the monolith. The team discovers that the Orders microservice needs data from the monolith's Customers module. What is the recommended approach during migration?
options: A. The Orders microservice should directly query the monolith's database to access customer data, using a read-only database connection
B. Create an Anti-Corruption Layer in the Orders service that calls the monolith's Customers API, translating between the monolith's data model and the microservice's domain model
C. Delay the Orders migration until the Customers module is also extracted as a microservice to avoid cross-boundary dependencies
D. Replicate the entire Customers database table into the Orders microservice using Change Data Capture

text: A cluster administrator applies a `MutatingWebhookConfiguration` that injects a sidecar container into every pod. The webhook has `reinvocationPolicy: IfNeeded`. Another mutating webhook modifies the pod's annotations after the sidecar injection. Under what condition does the sidecar injection webhook run again?
options: A. It runs again on every subsequent mutating webhook's modification, regardless of whether the changes affect the sidecar webhook's logic
B. It runs again only if the annotation changes made by the second webhook would cause the sidecar webhook to produce a different mutation than its first invocation
C. It runs again if any other webhook modifies the pod object after the sidecar webhook's initial invocation, allowing it to react to the changes
D. It never runs again because mutating webhooks are invoked at most once per admission request, regardless of `reinvocationPolicy`

text: A CSI driver supports volume snapshots. A `VolumeSnapshot` is created from a PVC that is actively being written to by a running pod. The snapshot `readyToUse` becomes `true`. Is the snapshot data guaranteed to be consistent?
options: A. Yes, the CSI driver quiesces I/O to the volume before taking the snapshot, ensuring application-level consistency
B. No, the snapshot is crash-consistent (like pulling the power plug) — data in flight or in application buffers at snapshot time may not be captured
C. Yes, Kubernetes freezes the filesystem using `fsfreeze` before the CSI snapshot call to ensure consistency
D. The consistency depends on the `snapshotClass` parameter `consistency: application` which must be explicitly set

text: A Gateway API `HTTPRoute` resource defines two `backendRefs`: Service A with weight 80 and Service B with weight 20. Both services have `readinessGates` configured. Service B's pods all fail their readiness checks and have no ready endpoints. How does the Gateway controller distribute traffic?
options: A. 80% to Service A and 20% is dropped with 503 errors because Service B has no ready endpoints
B. 100% to Service A because the Gateway controller automatically redistributes traffic away from backends with no healthy endpoints
C. The behavior depends on the Gateway controller implementation — the Gateway API specification does not mandate specific behavior for backends with no ready endpoints
D. The HTTPRoute becomes invalid and all traffic is rejected because the route references a backend with zero endpoints

text: A centralized logging system uses Loki for log aggregation. Labels assigned to log streams include `namespace`, `pod`, `container`, and `request_path`. After deployment, Loki's ingester reports `too many active streams` errors and high memory usage. Which label is causing the issue and why?
options: A. The `pod` label causes high cardinality because pod names include random suffixes that change on every restart, creating new streams
B. The `container` label creates redundant streams when pods have sidecar containers, doubling the stream count per pod
C. The `namespace` label is unnecessary since Loki automatically infers it from the log source path, creating duplicate streams
D. The `request_path` label has unbounded cardinality (unique URLs create unique label values), causing stream explosion; it should be a structured metadata field or removed from labels

text:
A cluster has the `PodTopologySpread` feature enabled. A Deployment with 6 replicas specifies:
```yaml
topologySpreadConstraints:
- maxSkew: 1
  topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
  whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
  labelSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
```
The cluster has 3 zones: zone-a (5 nodes), zone-b (2 nodes), zone-c (1 node). All nodes have available capacity. How does `ScheduleAnyway` affect pod distribution?
options: A. Pods are distributed 2-2-2 across zones because `ScheduleAnyway` still tries to honor `maxSkew: 1` as a soft preference
B. Pods are distributed based solely on available node capacity: 4 in zone-a, 1 in zone-b, 1 in zone-c
C. Pods are distributed 2-2-2 across zones, identical to `DoNotSchedule`, because the skew can be satisfied
D. Pods are distributed unevenly because `ScheduleAnyway` makes the constraint purely informational with no scheduling impact

text: A Kubernetes cluster uses RBAC. A user has a `ClusterRole` with `get`, `list`, and `watch` permissions on `secrets` in all namespaces via a `ClusterRoleBinding`. The security team argues this is equivalent to cluster-admin access for secrets. Are they correct, and why?
options: A. No, because `get`/`list`/`watch` only provide read access; the user cannot modify or delete secrets, so it is significantly less privileged than cluster-admin
B. No, because secret values are redacted in `list` and `watch` responses; only `get` on a specific secret returns the actual data

C. Yes, because `list` and `watch` on secrets returns secret data (values are included in list/watch responses), giving the user access to all secrets including service account tokens across all namespaces
D. Yes, but only if the user also has `get` permission on the `secrets/data` subresource, which controls access to the encoded values

text: A team uses Flux CD with a `Kustomization` resource that reconciles every 5 minutes. The Git repository has a `kustomization.yaml` that references a remote base from another repository. The remote base is updated with a breaking change. How does Flux handle this?
options: A. Flux detects the remote base change on the next reconciliation, applies the breaking change, and the application breaks in production
D. Flux's built-in kustomize controller validates remote base changes against a schema before applying, rejecting breaking changes
C. Flux pins remote bases to a specific commit SHA in the `kustomization.yaml`, so remote changes are only applied when the SHA reference is explicitly updated
B. Flux only watches the configured Git repository; it does not detect changes in remote bases unless the main repository's commit hash changes

text: A cluster runs `kube-proxy` in IPVS mode with `strictARP: true` in the `kube-proxy` ConfigMap. This setting was required after deploying MetalLB for bare-metal load balancing. What does `strictARP: true` do and why is it needed for MetalLB?
options: A. It prevents kube-proxy from responding to ARP requests for Service VIPs, allowing MetalLB to be the sole ARP responder for LoadBalancer IPs
B. It enables strict source IP validation in IPVS rules, preventing IP spoofing attacks on Service endpoints
C. It forces kube-proxy to respond to ARP queries only for its own node IP, not for Service ClusterIPs, preventing ARP conflicts with MetalLB's L2 mode
D. It configures the node's network interfaces to only respond to ARP requests for addresses assigned to the incoming interface, preventing multiple nodes from responding to MetalLB's VIP ARP

text: A pod with `restartPolicy: OnFailure` runs a Job. The container exits with exit code 0 (success). The kubelet observes the exit. What happens next, and what is the final pod phase?
options: A. The container is restarted because the kubelet always restarts containers in non-`Never` restart policies; the pod remains `Running`
B. The Job controller creates a new pod because it interprets the completed pod as requiring replacement to meet its `completions` target
C. The container is not restarted, but the pod phase stays `Running` with the container in `Terminated` state until the Job controller cleans it up
D. The container is not restarted (exit code 0 = success); the pod transitions to `Succeeded` phase and remains on the node until the Job TTL or manual deletion

text: A multi-cluster setup uses Cilium Cluster Mesh to connect two clusters. Cluster A has a Service `backend` in namespace `app`. Cluster B needs to access this service. Both clusters have their own `backend` Service in the `app` namespace with different backends. How does Cilium Cluster Mesh handle service discovery?
options: A. Cluster B's service takes precedence; local services always override remote services in Cluster Mesh
B. Cilium merges the endpoints from both clusters' `backend` services into a single global service, load-balancing across all endpoints from both clusters
C. The service names conflict and Cluster Mesh rejects the configuration, requiring unique service names across clusters
D. Each cluster maintains its own service namespace; cross-cluster access requires explicit `<service>.<cluster>` DNS entries

text: A team implements supply chain security for their container images. They need to: (1) sign images after build, (2) store signatures alongside images in the registry, (3) verify signatures at admission time in Kubernetes. Which combination of CNCF/ecosystem tools provides this end-to-end workflow?
options: A. Notary v2 for signing, Docker Content Trust for storage, and OPA Gatekeeper for admission verification
B. cosign (from Sigstore) for signing and registry storage, combined with Kyverno or a policy controller for admission-time verification
C. GPG signing integrated into the Dockerfile, stored as image labels, and verified by a custom validating webhook
D. TUF (The Update Framework) for signing and distribution, with Falco for runtime verification of image integrity

text: A Helm chart's `values.yaml` defines `replicaCount: 3`. A user installs the chart with `helm install myapp ./chart --set replicaCount=5`. Later, they run `helm upgrade myapp ./chart -f custom-values.yaml` where `custom-values.yaml` does not include `replicaCount`. What is the resulting `replicaCount` after the upgrade?
options: A. 5, because Helm preserves values from the previous release that are not overridden in the upgrade
B. 3, because the upgrade starts fresh from the chart's `values.yaml` and `custom-values.yaml` does not override `replicaCount`
C. 5 if `--reuse-values` is passed, or 3 if it is not; the default behavior resets to chart defaults merged with the provided values file
D. Undefined — Helm removes keys not present in the upgrade values, leaving `replicaCount` unset in the template rendering

text: An admission controller chain processes a pod creation request in this order: MutatingAdmission -> ValidatingAdmission. A mutating webhook adds a sidecar container. A validating webhook checks that all containers have resource limits. The sidecar injected by the mutating webhook does not have resource limits. What is the outcome?
options: A. The pod is created with the sidecar but without limits, because validating webhooks cannot see mutations from mutating webhooks
B. The pod is rejected by the validating webhook because it evaluates the final mutated object, which now includes a sidecar without limits
C. The pod is created because Kubernetes automatically injects default resource limits from the namespace's LimitRange for mutating webhook-injected containers
D. The mutating webhook's changes are rolled back when the validating webhook rejects, and the pod is created without the sidecar

text: A team uses Kubecost to analyze cluster spending. The report shows that 40% of costs come from `Unallocated` resources. What does `Unallocated` represent in Kubecost's cost model, and how should the team address it?
options: A. Resources consumed by pods without cost labels; the team should add `cost-center` labels to all workloads
D. Idle resources from pods that have requests but low actual utilization; the team should use VPA to right-size requests
C. Resources consumed by system components (kubelet, kube-proxy, OS processes) that are not tracked as Kubernetes workloads
B. The difference between total node capacity and the sum of all pod resource requests; the team should right-size nodes or increase workload requests to reduce waste

text: A Deployment specifies `revisionHistoryLimit: 2`. Over time, 5 rollouts have been performed (revisions 1 through 5). The current active revision is 5. Which ReplicaSets are retained, and what happens if the operator runs `kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>`?
options: A. ReplicaSets for revisions 3, 4, and 5 are retained; `rollout undo` reverts to revision 4
B. ReplicaSets for revisions 4 and 5 are retained (current + 1 history per limit); `rollout undo` reverts to revision 4, creating revision 6
C. ReplicaSets for revisions 3, 4, and 5 are retained (limit of 2 means 2 old + 1 current); `rollout undo` reverts to revision 4, creating revision 6
D. Only the ReplicaSet for revision 5 is retained; `rollout undo` fails because there is no previous revision available

text: A container image uses a non-root user (UID 65534) defined in the Dockerfile with `USER 65534`. The Kubernetes pod spec has `securityContext.runAsUser: 1000`. Inside the running container, what UID does the process run as?
options: A. UID 65534, because the Dockerfile `USER` directive takes precedence over the pod's `securityContext`
B. UID 1000, because the pod's `securityContext.runAsUser` overrides the Dockerfile `USER` directive at runtime
C. The container fails to start because there is a conflict between the image's user configuration and the pod security context
D. UID 1000 for the main process, but child processes inherit UID 65534 from the image configuration

text: A distributed system uses the Outbox Pattern to ensure reliable event publishing from a microservice that writes to a database. The service writes business data and an event record to the outbox table in the same database transaction. A separate process reads the outbox and publishes events to a message broker. What problem does this pattern solve compared to directly publishing events from the service?
options: A. It eliminates the need for a message broker by using the database as the event store, reducing infrastructure complexity
B. It solves the dual-write problem — ensuring that the database write and event publication either both happen or neither happens, preventing data inconsistency
C. It improves event publishing throughput by batching multiple events from the outbox table into a single broker publish call
D. It provides exactly-once event delivery by using the database transaction's ACID properties to guarantee each event is published exactly once

text: A CI/CD pipeline builds container images and pushes them with tags based on the Git commit SHA. The pipeline then updates a Kubernetes Deployment manifest in a separate GitOps repository by changing the image tag. This triggers Flux CD to deploy the change. Which CI/CD anti-pattern is present in this pipeline, and what is the risk?
options: A. The pipeline uses mutable image tags (commit SHAs are rewritten during force pushes), risking deploying a different image than intended

B. The pipeline pushes to the GitOps repo from the CI pipeline, creating a tight coupling between CI and CD; if CI credentials for the GitOps repo are compromised, attackers can deploy arbitrary images
C. The pipeline does not pin base images in the Dockerfile, risking supply chain attacks through base image updates between builds
D. The pipeline stores the image tag in a Kubernetes manifest instead of using Helm values or Kustomize overlays, making rollbacks difficult

text: A cluster administrator creates a `NetworkPolicy` that allows ingress to pods labeled `app: db` only from pods labeled `app: api` on port 5432. After applying the policy, the `api` pods can connect to `db` pods. However, the `db` pods cannot initiate connections to any other pod. No other NetworkPolicies exist in the namespace. Why are outbound connections from `db` pods blocked?
options: A. The NetworkPolicy implicitly blocks all egress because it selects the `db` pods, and any pod selected by a NetworkPolicy has a default-deny for unspecified policy types
B. The NetworkPolicy has `policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]` but only defines ingress rules; the empty egress section creates a default-deny for egress
C. The CNI plugin applies a default-deny-all policy to any pod that is the target of at least one NetworkPolicy, affecting both ingress and egress
D. The NetworkPolicy only has `policyTypes: [Ingress]`; the `db` pods' egress is blocked by the cluster's default network policy

text: An OpenTelemetry Collector is deployed as a DaemonSet. It receives traces via OTLP gRPC, processes them with a `batch` processor and `tail_sampling` processor, and exports to Jaeger. The team notices that trace sampling decisions are inconsistent — the same trace ID is sometimes partially sampled (some spans kept, others dropped). What is the architectural flaw?
options: A. The `batch` processor reorders spans before the `tail_sampling` processor, causing incomplete trace assembly
B. Tail-based sampling requires all spans of a trace to be evaluated together, but the DaemonSet deployment means spans from the same trace arrive at different collector instances on different nodes
C. The `tail_sampling` processor has a too-short `decision_wait` period, causing sampling decisions before all spans arrive
D. The OTLP gRPC receiver does not guarantee span ordering, causing the tail sampler to make decisions on incomplete traces

text: A team implements canary deployments using Flagger with Istio. The canary analysis runs for 5 iterations with 60-second intervals, checking error rate and p99 latency metrics. After 3 successful iterations, the 4th iteration detects an error rate spike. What does Flagger do?
options: A. Flagger pauses the canary and waits for manual approval to continue or rollback
B. Flagger immediately rolls back the canary by scaling it to zero and routing 100% traffic to the primary, then marks the canary as failed
C. Flagger retries the failed iteration up to the configured `threshold` count before initiating a rollback
D. Flagger reduces the canary's traffic weight by half and re-runs the analysis to confirm the issue before deciding on rollback

text: A platform team defines their cloud native maturity model. They categorize workloads into levels: Level 1 (containerized), Level 2 (orchestrated), Level 3 (observable), Level 4 (declaratively managed), Level 5 (auto-remediated). An application has automated scaling, health checks, structured logging with Loki, Prometheus metrics, distributed tracing with Jaeger, GitOps deployment with Argo CD, and self-healing via liveness probes. Which level does this application achieve?
options: A. Level 3 — the application has strong observability but lacks the declarative management to reach Level 4
B. Level 4 — GitOps with Argo CD provides declarative management, but self-healing via liveness probes alone does not constitute auto-remediation at the platform level
C. Level 5 — the application has all capabilities including auto-remediation through liveness probes and autoscaling
D. Level 4 — while it has observability and declarative management, auto-remediation requires integration between observability signals and automated response (e.g., Keptn quality gates)
